The Ordovician Period. Spanning from four hundred and eighty-five to four hundred and forty-four million years ago, the Ordovician saw an explosion of marine diversity as fishes emerged, corals and cephalopods flourished, and invertebrates colonised the seafloor. The period is named after the Ordovices, an ancient Welsh tribe. It ended abruptly with a mass extinction, possibly triggered by glaciation and ocean oxygen loss.

The Ordovician Radiation nearly tripled the number of marine families, diversifying the ocean into rich ecological zones. Jawless fishes, called agnathans, appeared for the first time, pioneering vertebrate life in the oceans. Cephalopods, ancestors of modern squid and octopus, rose to prominence as top predators, with some reaching ten metres long. Brachiopods and trilobites remained abundant, and corals and sponges built the first reefs.

The Ordovician extinction struck around four hundred and forty-four million years ago and stands as one of the Big Five mass extinctions, wiping out roughly eighty-five percent of marine species, likely due to glaciation and ocean anoxia—a lack of oxygen. Land remained barren during this entire period; all animal life was either marine or lived in freshwater.

This period follows the Cambrian, which established the first animal phyla, and precedes the Silurian, the period that followed the extinction event, and its defining feature was the ordovician radiation and the emergence of jawless fishes.
